newsitem.title: USA: U.S. against force to end coup in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. against force to end coup in Sierra Leone.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it opposed use of force by Nigerian-led West African peace-keeping troops to overturn last weekend's military coup in Sierra Leone, and called for a diplomatic solution.

Asked if the Nigerians should use force to restore democratic government in Sierra Leone, State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters: "There is no need. We would oppose any further violence."

He spoke as Nigeria flew in troops, jeeps and armoured personnel carriers for an expected regional intervention to restore President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, deposed Sunday by an Armed Forces Revolutionary Council.
There were signs that Ghana and Guinea would join in a possible intervention by the Nigerian-led ECOMOG peace-keeping force, which had troops in Sierra Leone before the coup.
Dinger said Washington had told Nigeria, whose military government has been criticised for years by the United States, that it wanted to see a peaceful outcome.

"We are using all possible diplomatic channels, both directly to the coup leaders in Sierra Leone, but also to our allies in the region and elsewhere to try to get them to urge the restoration of the civilian government in Sierra Leone," he said.
"We will continue to pursue all diplomatic efforts, including all international pressure possible, to restore the democratically elected government," Dinger added.
"There has been enough violence in Sierra Leone. We hope democracy is quickly restored there by diplomatic means and through international pressure."
U.S. marines using helicopters Friday evacuated some 900 foreigners fleeing violence in Sierra Leone to the warship Kearsarge standing off the coast.

Although the State Department this week praised the "useful role" of Nigerian troops in Sierra Leone, a U.S. diplomat made clear Friday fear of imminent military action was one reason the United States had closed its embassy there.

Ann Wright, charge d'affaires in Freetown, referred to "what appeared to be a Nigerian military operation to restore the former (civilian) government" as one of the factors that led to the decision to evacuate her and her colleagues.
